nameStory: Dotted watermeal gets its name from tiny dots or punctures visible on its surface when viewed under magnification. The 'watermeal' part comes from its grain-like appearance - these microscopic green specks floating on water look remarkably like cornmeal sprinkled across the surface. Early botanists thought these tiny dots resembled scattered meal or flour.
description: Dotted watermeal is the world's smallest flowering plant, so tiny you might not even notice it without looking closely. Each individual plant is a minuscule green speck, barely over a millimeter long, with no leaves, stems, or roots. It floats freely on the surface of still water, often forming dense green mats that look like algae from a distance. Despite its tiny size, it's actually a complete flowering plant with reproductive parts crammed into that microscopic package.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Impossibly small - each plant is only about 1.2 millimeters long, roughly the size of a pinhead or smaller than most grains of sand

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Oval-shaped with one rounded end and one pointed end, like a tiny green teardrop floating on the water surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms floating green mats on calm water that feel slightly slimy and break apart easily when touched

idTips.label: Structure
idTips.description: Completely rootless and leafless - just a simple green body with a flattened top surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Microscopic reproductive parts (one stamen and pistil) sit in a tiny depression on the flat top - invisible without magnification

habitat: Found floating on the surface of calm, still waters like ponds, quiet lake coves, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich water and often grows alongside duckweeds in protected areas where wind and waves won't disturb the water surface. Most commonly spotted in shallow, sun-warmed waters during the growing season.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin multiplying rapidly as water warms, though individual plants are so small they're easily overlooked among emerging aquatic vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when green mats are most visible and extensive, covering portions of quiet water surfaces in dense carpets.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into early fall in warmer water, but growth slows considerably as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back or become dormant in frozen water bodies, surviving as dormant buds or seeds to restart populations next spring.

funFact: Despite being the world's smallest flowering plant, dotted watermeal is completely edible and packed with protein - it contains more protein per unit than soybeans and has been harvested as food in some parts of the world for thousands of years!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be mistaken for algae or pond scum rather than other plants due to its tiny size. Unlike algae, watermeal plants are individual floating specks that can be separated from each other, while algae typically forms stringy or slimy masses. Memory trick: if you can pick out individual tiny green dots, it's probably watermeal; if it's all connected in strings or sheets, it's likely algae.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Wolffia honors German botanist Johann F. Wolff, while 'borealis' means 'northern,' referring to this species' preference for cooler northern waters. Many people are amazed to learn that something so microscopic can be a complete flowering plant with the same basic life cycle as an oak tree.
compareHints: Dotted watermeal is distinguished from its watermeal relatives by those characteristic tiny dots or punctures on its surface that give it its name. Brazilian watermeal and Columbian watermeal lack these distinctive surface markings and have slightly different shapes. All watermeals are incredibly tiny compared to their duckweed cousins in the same plant family, which have obvious leaf-like structures and roots.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Brazilian watermeal is virtually identical to its relatives Columbian watermeal and dotted watermeal, and they can only be reliably distinguished under a microscope by examining flower structure and surface texture details.
Columbian watermeal is nearly identical to other watermeal species and requires microscopic examination to distinguish definitively.
